utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are two witnesses listed for today. It is important that we conclude them both if at all possible. There are a number of administrative matters I should bring to your attention. Might it be convenient if I do that between the two witnesses, at which time I should have some speaking notes to make matters more efficient?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By way of forecast, however, there are two points. One is we will be filing today an application for safe conduct of a particular witness under Article 18 of the headquarters agreement. For timetable reasons we would be extremely grateful if that can have consideration by the Chamber as soon as possible, and I'll get that filed immediately. And it may help the Chamber to know that I'm going to invite you to consider fixing strict timetables of examination-in-chief and cross-examination for remaining witnesses so that we can know with certainty what witnesses can be accommodated rather than it being a matter evolving simply by passage of time. But I'll come to all those matters between the two witnesses. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution calls Mr. Nenad Zafirovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How long do you anticipate you might be?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I anticipate that I will take approximately 40 minutes in my direct examination. We will be admitting a number of paragraphs that are contained in the summary and I will notify the Court as I do that. Your Honour, while we are waiting for the witness to be brought into the Chamber could I ask that an exhibit number be assigned for a binder of five exhibits, that I could draw the Chamber's attention to a correction that needs to be made to the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, the next number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 632, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the summary that you've been provided under tab 5, it was a courtesy copy of Exhibit 538, tab 9. Overnight we've removed that from the bundle of exhibits and we've provided that separately. So what is listed as tab 6 in the witness summary is now 5, and 5 has been omitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would like to take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, can I ask you to begin your testimony by telling us your name.

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: My name is Nenad Zafirovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what is your profession?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: I'm a reporter, a journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask that the witness be shown tab 1 of Exhibit 632.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And, sir, can I draw your attention to the bottom right-hand corner and ask you is that your initials on the bottom of that page?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Does this document accurately record your professional and educational experience?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you now to turn to tab 2 of that same exhibit, 632.

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And are those your initials on the bottom of that page?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, those are my initials.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is my intention to lead all of the evidence today in open session. The witness has requested that the person whose name appears at the top of tab 2, if he be permitted to be allowed to refer to him as a JNA officer rather than call his name publicly in court because of concerns he has for this person's security. If that's acceptable to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I'm finished with the exhibits for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I want to draw your attention now to August of 1991. Did you have a conversation with the JNA officer that's listed in tab 2 of 632?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did talk to that officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you have a conversation with him regarding some events that had occurred in Erdut?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That in fact was the main topic of our conversation. We were discussing what was happening in Erdut over the past few weeks, and I was informed of the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you have a conversation with him regarding the destruction of the Catholic church there, and if so, did he tell you who it was that destroyed the church?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, because the first thing one sees on entering Erdut is the destroyed Catholic church. I asked him who had done it, and he answered that it had been done by soldiers of Zeljko Raznjatovic Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did he tell you whether or not he informed his superiors in the JNA about this act by Arkan's men?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He told me that he had informed them about it, and he also expressed his personal disapproval of this fact -- of this act.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did he also inform you about Arkan or Arkan's men arresting two of his men, JNA soldiers?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was referred to as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When did he say that Arkan's men arrested two of his soldiers, his JNA soldiers?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: I think this was in mid or end of August. These were regular soldiers of the Yugoslav People's Army, and according to this officer, they were taken to the auto centre or the headquarters of the Serbian Volunteer Guards in Erdut where they were detained, after which an officer of the JNA came with his units in front of this Alpha Centre in Erdut and asked or demanded Arkan to release these soldiers immediately, which he did. And according to this officer, he went with him to his command. Arkan apologised for the incident and promised that such things would not happen again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And this was in August of what year?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: August 1991, which is the first year of the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could ask the witness whether he had been aware of the reason for the -- Arkan's men to arrest the JNA soldiers at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did the JNA officer tell you or explain why it was his men were arrested?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: In his opinion, this was an attempt by Arkan to frighten the Yugoslav People's Army or, rather, the unit that was there and to show that he virtually controlled the area. This is not my opinion. This is what I heard from this officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, sir, is it true that you are familiar with Arkan's centre in Erdut and you have visited it -- or visited it during this period a number of times? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with the centre. Its name is Alpha. It was situated in the former wine cellar in Erdut. On one occasion with a group of journalists I entered the centre. It was a kind of promotional visit, and we were taken around several premises, places where members dined, and a short statement was given, and that was the first and last time that I had visited this centre in Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The JNA officer that relayed this account to you of his men being arrested, did he inform you of any corrective action or any action that the JNA took with respect to Arkan in regard to this incident?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't. And as far as I know, no measures were taken against Zeljko Raznjatovic Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, during the times that you were in the Erdut area near the Alpha Centre, did you ever see a person who was commonly known at that time as Captain Dragan?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is Dragan Vasiljkovic, also known as Captain Dragan. On several occasions passing through -- along the road going past the Alpha Centre I and some colleagues of mine would see Dragan Vasiljevic engaging in tactical exercises with members of the Serbian Volunteer Guard of Zeljko Raznjatovic Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: During the course of one of your visits to the Alpha Centre did you become aware that a person by the name of Jovica Stanisic was visiting the centre?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: I have to correct you. This wasn't during any visit to the Alpha Centre, but while staying in Erdut, we wanted to pass along the road leading to the Alpha Centre but it was blocked. A column of black vehicles went by and later, subsequently we learned that Jovica Stanisic was in one of those black vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you ever see a person by the name of Radovan Stojicic, commonly known as Badza, in the Erdut area or the area of the camp?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: No, not in the area of the Alpha Centre but in the area of Erdut, yes. On one occasion he came to visit a part of the armoured Mechanised Brigade of the JNA that was situated in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: During any of your trips to the Erdut area, did you ever cross a border that was guarded by members of Arkan's Tigers?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The bridge at Bogojevo, which actually separated the part of Serbia not swept by war and a part of Eastern Slavonia where there was a war, and on the Slavonia side of the bridge were members of the Serbian Volunteer Guard of Zeljko Raznjatovic Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And on how many occasions did you see them at that border crossing?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: I can't say with absolute certainty, but it must have been more than six or seven times.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would like to now draw your attention to April 1992, to the Bosnia municipality of Bijeljina. During that month did you, in pursuit of your work as a journalist, have occasion to go to Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the beginning of April when conflicts started in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to draw your attention specifically to the Serbian side of the border on your way to Bijeljina. Can you describe for the Chamber what if any armed forces you saw gathering on the Serb side of the border?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was several days prior to the events in Bijeljina. I think it was the 2nd of April, close to the frontier crossing at Sremska Raca. I was driving with a colleague towards Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I saw a member of Arkan's Serbian Volunteer Guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Approximately how many? Was it just one member or were there other members of Arkan's guards or Arkan's Tigers on the Serbian side of the border?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: I must say it was a group. There were several vehicles or, rather, jeeps. There was an armoured vehicle, a camouflage armoured vehicle, and the exact number of members of the guard I can't tell you, but I think there were more than 60 of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were the vehicles that you describe, did they contain any logo identifying the organisation that they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. SDG, standing for the Serbian Volunteer Guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I want to draw your attention to a period of time after you entered into Bijeljina. Were you present when Mrs. Plavsic and Mr. Abdic visited from the Assembly in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were you present during a meeting that was held in Bijeljina pursuant to their visit?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was present during part of the meeting between Mrs. Plavsic, Mr. Abdic, and Mr. Zeljko Raznjatovic Arkan, and Mr. Ljubisa Savic Mauzer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you briefly explain to the Chamber the circumstances surrounding your attendance at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: The circumstances were rather strange. As a journalist, I had managed to reach Bijeljina. We had heard that a delegation was coming from Sarajevo. At the time, Mrs. Plavsic and Mr. Abdic were members of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. They were members of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the reason that they were said to be coming was to calm down the situation and the conflict that had broken out in Bijeljina the previous night. The delegation arrived in Bijeljina, as far as I can remember around midday, they went to the Municipal Assembly building where they were met by Zeljko Raznjatovic Arkan, and Ljubisa Savic Mauzer was also present who introduced himself as a representative of the Serbs in Bijeljina and head of the Crisis Staff of Serbs in Bijeljina. And for unknown reasons that were never explained to us Goran Hadzic was also there, who at the time was the president of the Serbian Council of Eastern Slavonia. Also present were officers of the Yugoslav People's Army. I remember the presence of General or Colonel Jankovic whose units were in the barracks in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Drawing your attention specifically to a meeting held at that time, were journalists allowed unrestricted access to that meeting?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Journalists were given a photo-op at the beginning of the meeting, as it is known. There were several cameras and cameramen present, after which all the journalists were chased out. As this is a large room in the Municipal Assembly, I simply sat down in a corner, waiting to be thrown out, but this didn't happen, so I can say that it was actually by chance that I attended a part of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were you eventually thrown out of the meeting when your identity was discovered?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ljubisa Savic Mauzer, about 30 or 35 minutes later noticed me and asked me what I was doing there. I told him what my job was, and then he asked me to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask now that the witness be shown Prosecution -- Exhibit 632, tab 3. It is a videotape of approximately five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to ask you to look at this on the monitor before you, and I will ask you some questions during the course of it running.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, there seems to be a problem with the video. Just give me half a second in trying to get it to move.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, while we're waiting for the video to load, are you -- you've seen this video already; is that not true?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you showed it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And are you visible in the video?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, at a certain point in time you can see me passing along.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you to characterise for the Chamber the meeting that you observed while you were there; the respective roles of Arkan, of General or Colonel Jankovic as you refer to him, of Mrs. Plavsic, and of Mr. Abdic.

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: I have to say that the meeting evolved in an atmosphere of great tension, especially at the beginning. There was a serious dispute between Mr. Raznjatovic and Mr. Abdic. Raznjatovic accused Abdic and what he called the Muslim and Ustasha sides of arming the Muslims in Bijeljina. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. To corroborate that, he brought a pistol of a rather strange shape and green in colour, and Raznjatovic said it was a Croatian pistol, the Sokac model, and he accused Abdic that they had received it from the Croatian side. Abdic denied this, pointing out that this was a conflict between armed Serbs and Muslim unarmed inhabitants of Bijeljina. Raznjatovic rejected this and denied it. Mrs. Plavsic throughout tried to calm the situation down and appealed to both Raznjatovic and Abdic to do everything they could to bring the situation in Bijeljina back to normal. As regards representatives of the Yugoslav People's Army, they virtually didn't speak during the meeting. General Jankovic kept notes, but during the part of the meeting that I attended, he didn't say anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, the video is now playing. Can you see it on the monitor before you?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And is this the meeting that you have just described to the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I am going to ask that we watch it for a minute or two, and I will ask for it to be paused at a particular point and ask you to describe what we see in the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could you pause the video here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, we are now at 1 hour, 54 minutes, 32 seconds of the video. Can I ask you to describe who is the person sitting that can be seen in the frame?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: It is Mr. Fikret Abdic, at that time a member of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the man standing next to him is the commander of the Serbian Volunteer Guards, Zeljko Raznjatovic Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the gun that we can see on the table there, is that the green gun that you referred to in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is this rifle or pistol of strange shape that he called the Sokac model.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And where again did he say that he got this gun from, this painted green gun?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: He said that that rifle had been captured from one of the Muslims during combat the previous night, and he claimed that those rifles were obtained by Muslims from the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, before I conclude the running of the video, can you describe who is to Mr. Abdic's left in the video?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: On that side we see Mrs. Biljana Plavsic. She was to my right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: On my left is Mr. Zeljko Raznjatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And who sitting at the table was to Mr. Abdic's right? Who is on his right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: To the right of Mr. Abdic is one of the members of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We will conclude the video now at this time. Sir, can I draw your attention now to the talks that were held in Geneva in an attempt to resolve the conflict in Bosnia. There have been a number of witnesses who have testified about those talks. My questions to you are limited. First, did you cover those talks? Did you go to Geneva and cover what happened at those talks?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I spent in Geneva the time from June 1993 until sometime in November. Not all the time. I would be there on a stint for 15 or 20 days, after which I would return to Belgrade, or depending how long or how well the talks were proceeding.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: During the time that you covered those talks, did you have regular contact with members of the Bosnian Serb delegation to those talks?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had regular contacts with the members of the delegation of the Bosnian Serbs, and not only them but with members of all the three delegations including the delegation of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the delegation of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you to identify for the Chamber the most prominent members of the Bosnian Serb delegation with which -- with whom you had regular contact during the course of covering the Geneva talks.

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Practically throughout the negotiations the delegation of the Bosnian Serbs comprised Radovan Karadzic, at that time president of Republika Srpska; Momcilo Krajisnik, president of the Assembly of Republika Srpska; and Nikola Koljevic, at that time vice-president of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you, based upon your observations and your dealings with the Bosnian Serb delegation, what if anything you can say about their relationship with the accused, Mr. Milosevic, during the course of the Geneva talks? What interaction existed between them?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: First of all, the accused spent several days in Geneva on several occasions, and in those moments when he was present in Geneva, he was practically the head of the delegation of Bosnian Serbs. At those times, they were difficult to get in touch with, and from all information that I was able to gather as a journalist and the information available to my colleagues, the accused was the head of their delegation and everything depended on him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were you ever present with Mr. Karadzic when Mr. Milosevic contacted him by phone? Were you ever present in the room?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: I can say yes to that question. On one occasion, more precisely one morning, I went for a brief interview with Mr. Karadzic, and I wanted to get a statement from him regarding the events of the previous day. We sat down - there were also Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Koljevic in the same room - and at that moment the telephone rang in the office. Mr. Karadzic answered the phone, and he said, "Hello, Mr. President." At that moment, Mr. Krajisnik asked me to leave the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: During your discussions with the members of the Bosnian Serb delegation, how would they refer or by what term would they refer to Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Officially, on the record, they would address him "Mr. President," whereas in informal conversations he was referred to as The Big Boss or The Big Daddy.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now I want to draw your attention to Belgrade itself. During the course of this time period, were you also in Belgrade, working as a journalist?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In that period I lived and worked in Belgrade as a journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there ever come a time when you saw Mr. Krajisnik in Belgrade on an unannounced visit and have a conversation with him regarding why he was there?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: I can say yes to that question too. On one occasion, quite by chance, I met with Mr. Krajisnik. It was sometime -- somewhere in downtown Belgrade near the offices of Republika Srpska. I was surprised to see him, and I asked how come he was in Belgrade, because his visit had not been announced. And he replied that he was due to attend some talks in the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: As best you're able, can you fix a date on when you saw him, or a time period when you saw Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to give you a precise answer, but I think it could have been the very end of 1993 or the beginning of 1994, but again I can't be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was there another occasion when you saw General Ratko Mladic on an unannounced visit in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Again, in view of the numerous visits by foreign statesmen and other foreign officials to the accused, whose office was in downtown Belgrade in the so-called Presidency of Serbia, the agency for which I worked had duty service at the parking lot outside the building of the Presidency, and on one such occasion we saw Ratko Mladic coming out of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was this the Federal Presidency or the Serbian Presidency?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: It was the building of the Presidency of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I want to now draw your attention to Pale in May of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I could ask the director to prepare the ELMO I will ask that an exhibit be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, did you cover this 30th meeting of the Republika Srpska Assembly session that was held in Pale, in Jahorina in May of 1993?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I reported from that session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And were you present during the entire Assembly session?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: From its beginning until it ended in the small hours of the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were you aware or were you present when Mr. Milosevic addressed that Assembly?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: To your knowledge, how many times did Mr. Milosevic address that Assembly?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: He addressed the deputies for the first time in open session, and his speech was followed by the speech of the Greek Premier Constantin Mitsotakis. The second time he addressed the deputies of Republika Srpska in closed session, and according to some information that I'm not able to confirm, he again addressed them towards the very end of the session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that tab 5 of Exhibit 632 be placed on the ELMO. And, sir, if I could ask you to take the pointer that should be in front of you, I'm going to ask you to begin by describing to the Chamber what it is they're looking at, or what it is that is tab 5.

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: On this chart, you can see my drawing of the Jahorina hotel, which is a place where members of the JNA and families resided in a place which was the seat of the Republika Srpska. The place is called Rajska Dolina. Here you can see the press room --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, since you're pointing to things. You need to point on the original to your left for us to be able to see where you're pointing, okay? So if I could ask you just to point to your left.

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: I will start from the beginning. This is the entrance to the Rajska Dolina Hotel. This was the lobby. Right next to the entrance there was the designated press room, as it was known, with a couple of telephone sets and fax machines, and in addition to that, there was another room available to journalists for their use.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: To save time, perhaps if I could ask you to indicate particular points of interests that I think are of most assistance to the Chamber. Could I ask you to indicate the room in which the Assembly session -- where the Assembly met and in which the speeches were given. Can I ask you to point to that on the diagram

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: It is this large room here. It is practically a dining hall that had been adapted to house parliament sessions. This big table was designated for the Presidency of the Republika Srpska. Momcilo Krajisnik, then president of the Assembly, was seated in the middle. This is the roster from which the speakers addressed the Assembly, and this is the first row where high officials from Belgrade, including Greek guests, were seated. Slobodan Milosevic must have sat somewhere here. I cannot remember exactly whether it was on the left or on the right. The second row was also occupied by high officials, and the rest of the rows --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You've testified that Mr. Milosevic addressed the Assembly twice, once in open session, once in closed session. Can I ask you to point where the journalists were during his first address to the 30th Assembly? If you would just point to that at this time.

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: The journalists were towards the end of the hall on the left and on the right. They had their equipment located here for mixing, and they could obtain sound from the front part of the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when all the journalists were directed to leave that room, that the Assembly was going into closed session?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was after the first part of the session when a break was announced for dinner. And following that, the deputies returned to the room and resumed work, and perhaps one or two speeches later the Chairperson, Krajisnik, suggested that they move into closed session because the subject they were discussing was serious and confidential. That means that it was to be closed for the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were all the journalists required to leave the room?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. All journalists were requested to leave the room, as far as I remember. Only the camera of the Pale television station remained inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Where were the journalists made to stay during this second address in closed session by Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: The journalists were on these premises here. And since they were working in closed session, and this was a glass door here, two soldiers were positioned in those places to prevent anyone from entering. And the journalists were still able to see through the glass door who the speakers were and perhaps even what they were talking about, whereas a part of the journalists returned to the room next to the entrance of the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you were able to sneak a tape recorder back into and record a portion of Mr. Milosevic's speech that he gave in closed session?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: I did do that, but not directly, not myself. A couple of my colleagues and I availed ourselves of the opportunity when we saw some deputies coming out to the restrooms to ask them whether they would be willing to take a tape recorder back in, and they did, and thus we were able to record part of the speech of the accused when he addressed the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that Exhibit 632, tab 4 be now played. Sir, I'm going to ask you to listen to this and then identify whether or not it is the audiotape.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the convenience of the Court, I have provided the other exhibit, 538, tab 9, I believe, a courtesy copy of that and have marked on that the portion -- that's the official transcript that was received from the Republika Srpska government, and I've marked on that the portion of the speech that the Chamber will now hear on audiotape, and also included in the binder of materials is the -- another translation of the actual tape and the Chamber will note or be able to see that they do correspond. I'd ask that the tape be now played.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me clarify this. This tape is not the original one which the witness was able to get at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Perhaps if I could ask a few questions, Your Honours, and I'll be able to clear that up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, do you have -- what we're going to listen to now, is this the original tape that came out of that room?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, it is not the original tape. It is part of the material that was broadcast on the same day in a radio show within a broader programme about the session of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Before we hear the tape, can I ask a couple of questions. After getting the tape, did you go and participate in a radio show in which you played a portion of that tape?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely, although it was not immediately after I got the tape, because I got the tape around 2.00 or 3.00 o'clock in the morning, and the session lasted until 6.00 a.m. After the session was over, I sent another telephone report to my head office, and after that I returned from Pale to Belgrade, went to work, edited my report, and it was used in a broadcast that was made at 3.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My associate received yesterday documents under several tabs. He got them yesterday for today. But the final tab is 6. After that, I have no more documents. This is what we received yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you seem to be speaking about tab 9. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may be a bit confusing. If I can just restate what is now contained in the bundle of exhibits. Tab 4 is the transcript of this audiotape that we will now hear. I provided as a courtesy to the Court a copy of 538, tab 9, which is the official transcript by the Republika Srpska government of the same session, so that the Court can compare the audiotape plus the official transcript taken at the time of that closed session. I'd now ask that the tape be played. If the director can broadcast it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, is this an accurate -- fair and accurate copy of the tape as you recall it that was made of Mr. Milosevic's closed session remarks to the 30th session of the Republika Srpska Assembly?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And were you one of the journalists who made these remarks that were made in closed session? Were you one of them -- one of the journalists who published them shortly after they were made?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: I have already answered that question, and I can repeat. It was broadcast eight and a half, nine hours after the session of the Assembly of the Republika Srpska ended. So I don't know if we were the first, but we were among the first radio stations that broadcast this material.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, the final area that I'd ask you to deal with here today is to summarise your experience as an independent journalist working in Serbia during this time period. Can I ask you in a few sentences to describe what independence -- what ability independent journalists like yourself had to disseminate objective news and opinions about what was going on in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: I have to say that from my personal experience, I can say that I really was able to report freely and objectively on all events, including events in Bosnia and Herzegovina, primarily to the editorial policy of the -- of my employer at the time, and that is the Belgrade Radio 92. What might have been a problem was the fact that B92 radio was not very far reaching technically speaking, and many people in Serbia were not able to listen to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What was the area that B92 had the capacity to broadcast to?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: In the period we are discussing, B92 could be heard in downtown Belgrade and the immediate vicinity of Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we've considered how long you should have in light of the relatively short time which the Prosecution have had, and the answer is that you will have one hour, if you require it, for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I expected at least the hour and a half that was indicated here, because this witness was introduced as 92 bis. I didn't think the side opposite would spend any time on him at all. In any case, I will try to use my time rationally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So for the sake of rationality, let us clear up the issue where you left off the examination-in-chief, this notorious session. We saw an audio clip of the discussion where we could hear various views expressed at the session. I hope you understand this, Witness.

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: I think what we heard was your address to the deputies of the Assembly of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Of course. It was my address to them, because all of us who spoke, who took the floor at the Assembly, spoke to the entire audience, the entire room, and it is only one fragment of the discussion in which I propose arguments to the contrary to those that had been heard before regarding the adoption of the Vance-Owen Plan, and I am opposing arguments that were presented in favour of rejecting the plan. Do you understand that? Because you said a moment ago you followed the entire session from beginning to end.

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Of course I understand that, but, Your Honours, regrettably I was not able to follow the entirety of the session because part of it was closed to the public. I followed very closely the part which was open to the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, this small closed session resulted from a very fiery discussion that had taken place, if I remember correctly, and I hope that as one of the attending journalists you were there in the building all day.

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You know it was doubly closed. It was closed twice, in fact; once when the speaker of the Assembly asked the journalists to be removed for reasons of confidentiality, and the second time when members of the deputies' club were conferring upstairs, and Cosic, myself, Mitsotakis and the other guests were waiting downstairs. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that. I said at the moment when members of the deputies' club had their own private consultations there was a closed session downstairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That lasted for several hours, if you remember.

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: I cannot say with any certainty how long that took, by think it might have been for 60 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. There are records to show that, and I suppose there must be an audio recording, at least one, of this session from which you only took out a fragment, as you said. Don't you think that in fact it was the side opposite that took out this fragment from the broader material that is available to them?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I must say that the segment that was played here was played in the radio show Interview of the Day of Radio B92. The segment that you heard was my own selection, made at that point in time when I compiled this for the radio show. So the opposing side or, rather, the OTP simply used material from that 60-minute broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Lest there be any confusion, the entire Assembly session, including the comments of all of the participants, not only Mr. Milosevic, are already in evidence as Exhibit 538, tab 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, though the witness is making the point -- or the accused is making the point that we haven't heard all of it. Maybe that's a good thing. But let's go on. I think we've got the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, on the basis of what we did hear a few minutes ago, I followed the transcript as I was listening, it is my voice, indeed. It is part of the arguments that I presented as to why the Vance-Owen Plan should be accepted, but it makes sense when what was said previously is heard as well. So the arguments presented then have to do with what was said previously. And I heard my own voice when I said we came to the conclusion together when we were from -- when we were in Geneva, Cosic, Karadzic, Bulatovic, Owen, Vance and others were in Geneva. There are lots of dots -- or, rather, there is not enough punctuation but you as a journalist can see that. Anyway, we observed with our constitutional lawyers there isn't a confederation in the world with fewer powers than Bosnia-Herzegovina. So fears were voiced, had been voiced that Serbs would be unequal, that this would be something that would not be good for the Serbs, and so on and so forth. And that is why I'm referring to this. That is why I'm saying that there is not a single man in uniform. And this reference is made to Bosnia-Herzegovina. There is not a single policeman, there is not a single soldier, there is not a single administrative organ. Everything is within the provinces; the police, the army, the administration, the judiciary, transportation, the economy, et cetera, everything, and so on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You are asking questions of the witness. You're not doing that, you're making a speech. What is the question you want to put to the witness? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not making a speech. I'm just trying to -- I mean, this is what was played by the witness himself here. This is what the witness played here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So then I'm talking about foreign policy. And the point is -- is this clear to you, Mr. Zafirovic? I say that a lever was provided that has the absolutely same importance and bears the same weight as the others. So the Serbs are equal there. They have equal rights. And then I give an example. Probably Radovan Karadzic, together with Alija Izetbegovic and Mate Boban, because these are the three leaders of the three communities, since foreign policy is a common one, then they will go to the conference in Iceland together because they constitute the Presidency. And then I explained therefore, they have equal rights. They are equal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, it's time that you were -- let the witness answer. You're not giving evidence at the moment. Now, do you -- do you agree -- let the witness answer what it is you're putting.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, Islamic conference rather than Iceland conference.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's not for me to agree or disagree. As far as I can understand the point of this testimony, I'm supposed to answer questions related to events that I attended, and what the accused is doing now is presenting a political opinion. If you ask me to give an answer to that, I shall do so, but I do not think that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- There's a question--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you have got anything useful to add, say so. But he's conducting himself, and he is allowed, to some extent, the right to ask questions but he's not entitled to speak all the time. Now, if you've got anything useful that you wish to answer to what's put so far, answer it or we'll go back to his asking questions. But if you'd like to say something, of course you've got the opportunity to say so now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I really have no comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Since this was taken out of context, I would like to repeat, Mr. May, Mr. Robinson, Mr. Kwon. I received this yesterday afternoon from my associate, all of this that was provided. There is tab 5 over here. Mr. Groome singled it out, and it is the very same text, and this excerpt was taken from there. So since you all received it just like I did, I would like to draw your attention to that as well. I have the Serbian text here. I see that it says 45, 44, pages 44, 45. Mr. Zafirovic, I assume you got the same thing that I got.

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not get a transcript of the entire speech made by the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Far be it from the entire speech. Pages were simply plucked out at random, a page or two. I'm just talking about the tabs that I got. I assumed that you received them too.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness was not provided a copy of Exhibit 538.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you got a copy now for him in case there is something he might wish to answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Now, what is it that you want to ask the witness about, Mr. Milosevic? What page? Perhaps you could ask him that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, what was played a few minutes ago shows this same text. It says a lever was given which has the same weight, the same importance as others. What is referred to are the powers shared by all three communities in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is what was quoted from Mr. Zafirovic's tape, this very same text which is on a page that has an ERN number in Serbian. And towards the end, this sentence was given, a lever was given with the same weight and the same importance with others. It shows that it is the very same tiny segment of the speech that was extracted here. So it's on this very same page. In that speech, it says with wise behaviour and sensible action in that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So is it clear to you, since you followed the session, that that is precisely what I advocated and Cosic and Mitsotakis and Bulatovic and others? What we were advocating was based on the fact that Serbs had achieved an equality of rights. This Vance-Owen Plan guaranteed peace, and that's why it should be accepted. So the insert that you refer to is an insert through which I am debating with them and some of their positions, because I'm saying that they live in a delusion as far as the importance of the plan is concerned. And then I say, "Do not say that the Serbs will not be equal --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. The witness should have a chance to answer these various points that you are making. Is there anything you want to add to what's been suggested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can only say as a journalists who followed the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina I am aware that the Vance-Owen Plan would have brought peace to Bosnia-Herzegovina. By your leave, I would like to explain why it is precisely this clip that you heard was played in the radio B92 broadcast, if you allow me to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You could certainly, the matter has been raised, but if you could deal with it fairly briefly, please, because the accused's time is limited, but certainly for some matter you wish to raise, of course you can do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'll be very brief. The reason why we decided to play precisely this material in the radio programme is the fact that the accused, when addressing the Assembly of Republika Srpska, used the word "we," not "you" as the Republika Srpska but "we." And that was quite different to what the accused was stating otherwise, that Serbia was not involved in the war. It is a fact that B92, by playing this recording, wanted to show that the accused was in a way involved in what was taking place in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, great, Mr. Zafirovic. Thank you very much for having put it this way. My entire approach at this session was that peace was in the greatest interest of all Serbs. And I said that on several occasions during that session, and that can be seen from the transcript. For all Serbs, Serbs in Bosnia, Serbs in Serbia, Serbs everywhere, regardless of where they are. And since I am a Serb, of course I say "we." And when I criticise certain positions, I say "you." And as far as peace is concerned, the issue of peace, which was of utmost importance for all Serbs, of course I say "we" because I'm a Serb. This is what can be read on this particular page. I'm not going to quote this yet again, what you quoted just now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Allow the witness to respond to your comment. If there's anything you want to add to what the accused has put, then of course you can answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, since there wasn't a question involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now on the following page, 02191, the last figures are 0191, I keep referring to the arguments against the plan in order to voice my approve of the plan. And then I say many have spoken about things that I absolutely cannot agree with. Many advocated the rejection of the plan, and they pointed out that war had been imposed upon us so that we could defend ourselves. Who is challenging that? Of course war was imposed on the Serb people. They had to defend themselves. And who was bringing that into question, that war was being imposed? But what else did the Serb people do? Had they not defended themselves, there would have been Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. no such plan. That is the point. And then I state that explicitly. That is an argument in favour of the opposite, that this plan should be accepted. That is what is written here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, wait a moment. The witness must have a chance to answer the comment if he wishes to. Yes, Mr. Zafirovic. If you wish to answer, do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, indeed I have nothing to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is part of the clip that we're talking about. And then I say in order to confirm exactly the issue that you raise now, since I'm discussing peace in the first person plural, because it is in the interest of all Serbs. I say: "We are either going to make senseless sacrifices, and who has the right to do that on behalf of the people? So that is not the question that is being put here, whether we are going to die slower or faster, because people who spoke against the plan said that this was a plan for dying. That is not the question. The question is whether to die or whether to live, and living implies living in peace." So that is what it says here. It is quite clear why, and I believe that even today everybody believes that the primary interests for all Serbs then and now is and was peace. And of course this pertains to Serbs in Serbia and Serbs in Republika Srpska and so on. I'm not going to go into the economic references made, and so on and so forth. I'm just going to say when I'm saying "you", finally I say: "Do not tell us that you feel abandoned." Because we insisted that they should accept the plan. And then some of them say, "We feel abandoned, you're not supporting us, et cetera." And I say, "Do not say that you feel abandoned. We who shared all your concerns all this time. Serbia did its utmost to help at a great cost to the population of Serbia, the 10 million inhabitants of Serbia, but do not say that you feel abandoned, because that is not fair." And then, since there's an interruption there, two pages were simply taken out, then there is an English page here, 0204 are the last numbers, and that is where the speech ends. [In English] "Is the Assembly going to decide on the reasonable way or the unreasonable way to the goal? I do not think that anybody should convince this Assembly about this, because I think that peace is the reasonable way. On the other hand, only the crimes against the Serbs can be achieved under the slogan that only the Serb does not wish peace. I think that this must be taken into consideration. This is why I think that now, when the road towards peace opens, you cannot explain to your people more massive brutality than during the entire war so far. You cannot explain that to either the people of Republika Srpska or the people in Serbia. In the end, I wish to tell you and I urge you to remember this: Everything needs to be sacrificed for the people except for the people themselves. You cannot sacrifice the people and you have no right to do that, either as the Assembly or as anything else." [Interpretation] So all of this is fragmented, and I assume that it can be seen that the point, the central issue is peace only. Therefore --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, it's high time -- high time that the witness has a chance to answer. Wait a moment. Wait a moment. Now, let the witness -- let the witness answer. You've written out -- or read out a large part of written material. The witness must have a chance.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is what I received from you last night. I am reading from your document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness answer. It's not just you alone. Now, do you want to say anything or not?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's up to you, Mr. Zafirovic, whether you do or not, but if you want to say something, you should have the opportunity to add anything.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I really have nothing to say.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll try to speed things up, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zafirovic, I received your statement. I assume you're familiar with it as it is yours.

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it occurred to me that having read out so much of that speech you should have put a specific question to the witness to drive home the point that you're making, which it seems to me is that you were seeking to promote peace, but the witness has not made any comment on it because you haven't asked him a specific question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I hadn't finished my sentence because once again Mr. May interrupted me. The witness explained that this segment was played by him because I was speaking in the first person plural, because I was saying "we," which he feels is proof, as he said, that it was not true what we were saying, that Serbia was not at war, because I was saying "we." However, reading out those excerpts from the speech, I'm proving that we were -- I was saying "we" because peace is in the interests of all Serbs. And I say that in my speech, the Serbs in Republika Srpska and the Serbs in the Republic of Serbia. You cannot explain to any Serbs anywhere anything if you reject peace. And I am saying "we" because peace is in the interest of all Serbs and because I am a Serb, and that is quite clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Continue with your questioning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zafirovic, I will quote from your statement now. I assume you agree with what you said in that statement because it is your statement and you are a professional who sought to do so as well as you could. At the end of your statement, if you would like to look at the last page. It is page 8 in my copy in the Serbian language "As regards atrocities, it is my professional opinion that the leadership of Republika Srpska, Krajisnik, Plavsic, and especially Karadzic, knew about them and did nothing to stop them. In my judgement the largest number of crimes in Croatia and Bosnia were committed by local people against their neighbours. The leadership of Republika Srpska just stood aside and let the locals commit the atrocities. They did nothing to stop them. This opinion of mine is based on my numerous interviews with leaders, soldiers, people, and -- I had during my travels as a journalist throughout Bosnia." Therefore, Mr. Zafirovic, you explained something that I assume you will confirm, but tell me whether you do or not, that this explanation of yours is actually a definition of something that is called a civil war. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I fully stand by the statement I gave, including the part read out by the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Since you mention here only Krajisnik, Plavsic, and Karadzic, you're just mentioning the Serb leaders in Bosnia, and yet you're talking about a phenomenon of crimes being committed mostly among neighbours, et cetera. I assumed that you also monitored the crimes committed against the Serbs. Again, between neighbours directly or by various units which you must have heard of covering the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina all that time; is that right, Mr. Zafirovic?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, as a reporter I reported on all events, including crimes committed against Serbs and crimes committed against non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you spoke to officials of Republika Srpska, you mention also soldiers and officers, et cetera, did you have any knowledge about formations such as the Green Berets, the Patriotic League, the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the armija as it was called, various paramilitary formations, the Mujahedin units that you probably had occasion to see a video story about, the review made by Alija Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Izetbegovic of that -- of those units with the Mujahedin. What do you know about those things, Mr. Zafirovic?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: I did know of the existence of the Patriotic League, the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but in those days, I didn't have any knowledge of Mujahedin units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When did you learn about the existence of those Mujahedin units and various other terrorists that have become so popular since the 11th of September?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: I learnt about Mujahedin units after the end of the war and the signing of the Dayton agreements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The knowledge that you acquired, does it enable you to answer my question, and that is what would roughly be the number of those warriors that were waging war, cutting people's heads off and -- throughout Bosnia and having their photographs taken with those heads and putting them in ammunition boxes? How many of them were there in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I really am unable to give a precise answer to this question since, as I have already said, I learnt about this from the media after the end of the war, and I have no specific information about those people nor their number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, what information do you have about the forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina during the time that you covered the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina; that is, the units that were waging war against the Serbs? What knowledge do you have about that?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: What I can say is that I knew of the existence of the Patriotic League, the Green Berets, and of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. As to the exact number of members of those units, I had no information. But compared with a number of members of the army of Republika Srpska, these were much fewer and more poorly armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How did you establish that they were far fewer in spite of opinion clearly expressed which you must be familiar with as a journalist that the fears that some witnesses even testified about on the part of the leadership of Republika Srpska were prompted by the fact that the Muslim forces were far more numerous, and they used this as an argument even when talking to representatives of UNPROFOR who testified here, saying that they couldn't pull back the artillery because the far more numerous Muslim forces could commit massacres in Serb areas which they were protecting. Where did you get the idea from that they were less numerous, that is members of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were fewer in number?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I stand behind what I said, and that is that at the beginning of the war and well into the war units under the command of the government in Sarajevo were fewer and drastically less well-armed than units of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you tour the units of the army?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're going to adjourn now. It's time for the break. Would you tell the witness, as far as the witness is concerned, don't speak to anybody of course about your evidence until you've finished. Mr. Milosevic, you've got another 25 minutes to cross-examine this witness. We will adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, before I resume, could you please give me some more time, because for a 92 bis witness who isn't testifying live at all, you give me usually an hour, and Mr. Zafirovic testified live for almost an hour, so I think I should have a little more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will consider that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've had to make a decision on the matter. It is this, that you have an extra ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me try and cover at least a few more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zafirovic, you mentioned the negotiations in Geneva that you covered; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Three delegations were negotiating over there; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The Serb delegation and heading it was Karadzic. Heading the Bosnian Croats was Mate Boban, and heading the Muslim delegation was Alija Izetbegovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As for my presence and the presence of Mr. Bulatovic, the presence of Mr. Tudjman, we would come exclusively at the invitation of Cyrus Vance and David Owen. I assume you're aware of that. And later at the invitation of David Owen and Thorvald Stoltenberg when Vance, after what we discussed in 1993 left this position, and Mr. Stoltenberg was appointed in his place. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that we were invited to attend those negotiations of theirs precisely in order to assist in achieving an agreement among the three negotiating delegations; that is, the delegation of Republika Srpska, the delegation of Herceg-Bosna, the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna at the time, and the delegation of Alija Izetbegovic, the Muslim delegation?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: I can answer in the affirmative.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on those occasions and in contact with those delegations and at the plenary meetings it was we who urged and endeavoured - and David Owen testified to that effect and I hope that Thorvald Stoltenberg will be able to come too - to help in achieving peace as soon as possible?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: That was the idea behind your presence as represented by the co-chairman.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In that case, there's no need to go into that matter any further. Let me move on, then, to your statement. You worked for the newspaper Vreme, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was an associate, a stringer. I wasn't a full-time employee.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Your colleagues Dulovic and Dejan Anastasijevic testified here. You know them, don't you?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How do you explain the fact that three journalists testifying here, all three were working in Vreme?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, as I have already said, I was never employed by the weekly Vreme but I would occasionally write for that weekly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. On page 2 of your statement, you say that you did your military service in 1991 and that later you became a reservist; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: I served my regular military service in 1985, 1986, and I later became a reservist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. And were you called up or mobilised in 1991 as a reservist?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: The answer is in the affirmative, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you voluntarily desert the JNA or had you completed your term?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: No. I had a back injury. After that, I was transferred to hospital, and after that I was discharged from service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And it was only then that you started working as a journalist covering the war?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: No. Before I was mobilised, I had already been covering the events in Eastern Slavonia. And after returning from the front, I continued to cover those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the first paragraph I see you say that you were never a member of the Serbian Democratic Party. In the second paragraph, I beg your pardon. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: That is right; I never was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand why you stress that in your statement. Were you asked about it by the investigators or did you yourself want to state that?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: No, the investigator asked me that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you ever a member of any other political party?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Which?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: The Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you say you were a member of the Democratic Party, in your statement here you mention Mauzer when talking about Bijeljina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that he too was a member of that party of yours? He was, because he is no longer alive. In fact, in the mid-1990s, he was leader of the Democratic Party for Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that, because really I don't have such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Since you spoke about these various paramilitary formations, I assume you remember well that the leadership of Serbia and I personally advocated support for the JNA. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a declarative support.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the paramilitary units were mainly formed by various opposition parties, the SPO and Mauzer's Serbian Guard, as you know yourself.

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: I can confirm what the accused said regarding the SPO, but as for Mauzer's Guards, I don't know that it was formed as a party paramilitary army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This unit that he had in Bijeljina at the time that you are talking about was called the Serbian Guards, and there are articles in the press, I even think in your own paper, about this. And then later, according to information collected by my associates, they came to be called the Panthers after their commander who was killed and whose surname was Pantelic. But during the time that you're testifying about, they were known as the Serbian Guards.

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: According to information I received from the late Mauzer, this was a combined unit of the Territorial Defence formed by the Crisis Staff in Bijeljina, and the subsequent name Panthers was acquired when the unit was attached to the regular forces of the army of Republika Srpska, which was headed by General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. When talking about Mauzer, you say that he was Minister of the Interior of Republika Srpska. I'm sure you must have found out that this was incorrect, because he was never Minister of the Interior of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm what the accused has said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Speaking about the events in Bijeljina, I wish to draw your attention to your statement on page 4, paragraph 2 -- or the third paragraph if you count the one carried over from the previous page. "It seemed to me that Mauzer was the person who had the greatest control over paramilitary units that had captured Bijeljina." And last sentence in the same paragraph: "I think that Mauzer was the person who was most responsible for the killings and destruction in Bijeljina." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that he even gave money to Arkan for him to come and assist his forces in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And do you know of Mauzer's statement from those days in Bijeljina -- I cannot claim for certainty that it appeared in your newspaper, but in anyway in one of the Belgrade papers, I think it was yours, Vreme, but I'm not a hundred per cent sure, and he was interviewed by a reporter about the events and then he says, "Now we fix these, and once we've done with them, we will cross the Drina to deal with the communists and fix them." Do you remember that statement?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Very superficially. I'm unable to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But do you remember a position to that effect roughly?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So Mauzer and the people around him were, in any event, against the authorities in Serbia; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: That is a question I cannot answer because I don't have precise information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. If you don't have precise information, I won't press you any further about that. You mentioned an officer of the JNA. Mr. Groome pointed out that his name shouldn't be mentioned because he could be at risk, though

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is going well beyond anything that we should be -- We will go into private session for this part of the hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I ask the Court to inquire of the witness whether the biographical information that has been discussed openly would compromise the person's identity in his opinion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Certainly the witness can deal with that question if he wants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So in April 1992, you were in Sarajevo, and you say that's when the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: However, on the same page, the same paragraph, you speak about shots heard from the background on one of your tapes, and you say it was the time of the siege in February 1992.

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The answer is yes. I was in Sarajevo on both occasions, in February and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was it that was happening in February? What kind of shots occurred in February 1992?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: If I may remind the accused, Your Honours, it was the siege of Sarajevo by Serb civilians or paramilitary units. It has never been clearly established. Sarajevo was under siege for ten or 12 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you saying Sarajevo was completely blocked for a couple of hours?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The formal reason for the blockade was the shooting at Bascarsija and the murder, the assassination of a member of a Serb wedding party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you mentioned this shot heard in the background on one of your tapes, how can you say who it was who fired the shot?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: I was there myself and that tape was recorded by me. A group of civilians had set out towards one of the barricades at a distance of about 600 metres from the Holiday Inn hotel in the centre of Sarajevo. That's where members of Serb forces, of Serb units, I don't know what to call them, were located, and Serb soldiers fired into the air.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But nobody was killed then? They did not shoot into the crowd?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: They did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the blockade was instituted in response to the assassination of a Serb during that wedding party at Bascarsija?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was the formal reason given for the blockade of downtown Sarajevo, Bascarsija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
