utterances.text: What do you call "formal" in that case? It was an assassination in the context of political events. Serbs were very upset. They thought to themselves, "They started killing us already. We need to do something."

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm being asked to speculate, and I don't want to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, who created these tensions in the first place? Do you know that? Was it the Serbs or the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: I cannot give you a precise answer. The situation was already rather tense even before that event.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. On the 4th of April, you were in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Plavsic and Mr. Abdic arrived in their capacity as members of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: I said so a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you suppose or do you know that somebody authorised them to go there? Because the president of the Presidency was Alija Izetbegovic; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they came on behalf of the Presidency to a place where an inter-ethnic conflict broke out between Serbs and Muslims, and two members of the Presidency, one Serb, one Muslim, arrived. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I suppose they had good intentions. They wanted to respond to that conflict in Bijeljina, and this Serb person, a Muslim, members of the Presidency, wanted to calm the situation down.

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I suppose that was the main reason for their visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did they succeed in calming the situation down, which lasted for a very short time? The conflict was very short-lived, and things returned to normal very quickly. After that there were no further incidents. Is that your information too?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: At that moment when Mrs. Plavsic and Mr. Abdic were in Bijeljina, the situation had indeed calmed down, but tensions remained in the immediate vicinity of Bijeljina in a village called Janja, which had a majority Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is to put it mildly, majority Muslim population. It was almost purely Muslim.

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: I can agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were no conflicts and there were no casualties, or maybe you've had different information.

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: According to the information I have, nobody was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You described here a quarrel between Abdic and Arkan, and you said that Arkan, as I saw in one of these transcripts I have been served, was accusing the Croats. But from what I can see in the transcript, Arkan was not speaking of Croats, he was speaking of Ustashas.

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the term Raznjatovic used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But I suppose that you, as everyone else, make a distinction between Croats and Ustashas. We're not talking about Ustashas as a derogatory term for Croats, we're talking about a specific group called Ustashas.

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is not a topic I can testify on, and I would not like to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm mentioning this only because this term is treated as a derogatory term to denote all Croats, and I don't agree with that. Nobody uses "Ustasha" as a term applying to all Croats.

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: I cannot say, Your Honours, what Arkan meant by saying "Ustashas." Did he mean all Croats or maybe the members of the Ustasha movement from the Second World War? So I cannot answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So you attended that meeting, and then you were thrown out of it. I don't quite see how this was done, because from your statement, I seem to understand that when they found out you were there, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you were chased out. You say: "I was interrogated by Ljubisa Savic, nicknamed Mauzer, who mistreated me." And you say here -- what you said here is that he kindly asked you to leave. Could you explain that?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: I had an argument with Ljubisa Savic Mauzer after I was thrown out of the meeting. The terms used were not mild.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But it was not that kind of atmosphere where journalists would be mistreated.

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Well, in my own opinion, I don't think the journalists were very welcome on that day in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's quite a different matter. I asked you whether you were mistreated.

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Verbally, yes; physically, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that after this discussion, you were banned from entering the territory of Republika Srpska for another four months.

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, could the accused be asked to specify after which discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Immediately after the paragraph from which I quoted a moment ago. It says: "RS, Republika Srpska therefore, banned me from entering its territory for another four months." It must have been after your visit to Bijeljina on that occasion because it's in the same paragraph. I supposed you understood what I was driving at.

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: No. This did not happen immediately after Bijeljina. That happened in the later months of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it had nothing to do with Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: No. The answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You mentioned people in the territory of Serbia, and you mention helicopters, 110 persons. I suppose those people were guarding the border, if you're referring to the police of the Republic of Serbia. No one from the Republic of Serbia, apart from that group headed by Mauzer, ever took part in the conflicts in Bijeljina. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: I can confirm that on that day in Bijeljina, I didn't see anyone from the MUP of Serbia. That much is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you understand from the video recording that you were shown and from the overall conduct when that delegation arrived to respond to the conflict between Serbs and Muslims, there was no intervention in the conflict? The conflict was dealt with, and tensions were dispelled.

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: I have said so once, and I will repeat: The JNA did not get involved in the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking, in that barracks of the JNA, there was just a small group of soldiers who discharged mainly logistical duties. They had no serious tasks of other natures.

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that because the press was not allowed into the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But you say on page 4, the penultimate paragraph: "I was not allowed to visit the JNA barracks in Bijeljina where, as I heard, the JNA accommodated refugees."

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the JNA was taking care of people, refugees, and allowed them to be put up in their barracks to protect them from possible danger; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So if we look at this as a whole, the events in Bijeljina, including what you said yourself, namely that Mauzer and his unit played the main part in this, the so-called Serbian Guards, and Arkan who was also there according to the testimony of some people who were here. My information is that he had ten men with him, some others say that his unit consisted of 60 people. Can I ask you if you can remember how many men were in the unit of Zeljko Raznjatovic Arkan?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would abide by my statement that there were around 60 based on their overall deployment in town. I did not count them, but my impression was there were about 60.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say yourself there was no one from the police of the Republic of Serbia, the JNA remained neutral, and then you say that Mrs. Plavsic who had arrived there with Mr. Abdic to calm the situation down. Plavsic, Krajisnik, and Karadzic together planned this conflict in Bijeljina. How did you arrive at this assertion?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Can I be guided a little? Where can I find this statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may assist. Page 4, the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "In my professional opinion as a journalist, Krajisnik, Karadzic, Mladic and Plavsic knew about these events and participated in their planning together with Milosevic." Don't you think this assertion is pretty absurd?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: I must say, Your Honours, I gave my statement in the English language, which is not my native tongue, and some parts of it may have been misinterpreted. I mentioned this possibility to the OTP as well. Some of the things I said, namely, were not conveyed truthfully.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, then. Tell me now about this paragraph on page 5 which sounds illogical to me. It may also be a question of translation. I will read it out to you. It's only four lines long. The penultimate paragraph. "Milosevic and Krajisnik were very close. I remember that on one occasion I asked Krajisnik why he was in Belgrade. He said that he was supposed to talk to the Minister of Interior. He talked to the minister and left Belgrade soon after. This was unusual because the government in Belgrade had not announced this visit to the media. I ran across Krajisnik purely by chance." Now, tell me, when you ran across him and he told you he was meeting the Minister of the Interior, how did you conclude that Krajisnik and I were very close?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I already explained about Mr. Krajisnik and my meeting with him. I can add that from the sources I had as a journalist, I received information that Krajisnik and the accused were close. The information is put together in such a way that it does not reflect the length of my interviews with the Office of the Prosecutor, but the sentence as it stands here is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, that is really -- I just wish to clarify some other issues that I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say in the last paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: My last statement was not interpreted for some reason. What I said was the accused has two minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say: "I recall that the leaders of Republika Srpska met in Jahorina in May 1993." That is the Assembly that we discussed. "And the Assembly decided to reject the plans. I remember that Plavsic was not present." If you attended the Assembly, as you said, how can you say that Biljana Plavsic was not present at the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, obviously there is a major misunderstanding involved here. The text that the accused has before him is my first statement, and afterwards I corrected it also in terms of Mrs. Plavsic's presence, because there was a small scandal, as a matter of fact, just before the Assembly started between the accused and Mrs. Plavsic. Of course I know that Mrs. Plavsic was at the Rajska Dolina Hotel on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to have that established, that this is an assertion that is wrong, but you explain it to be a mistake. All right. Just one more question that seems to very important to me. On page 6, you say: "As regards the existence of concentration camps in Republika Srpska, I remember that I asked Plavsic and Karadzic about that. Karadzic said that he did not know about the existence of the camps and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. declared that he would investigate." This is the first time I see that someone is testifying about something that Karadzic said to me and that had I been claiming all along, that Karadzic said to me that there were no concentration camps, and apparently he said the same thing to you. When was it that he told you that in response to your question?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: I cannot give you the exact date, but I think it was the end of 1993 and the beginning of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So had he known anything about it, he would have had to know at least by then in 1993/1994; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: I put the question to Mr. Karadzic in an interview, and that's the answer he gave me. That's the only thing I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now I'm interested in something that I come across for the first time here. So far, I haven't heard anything like that from anyone. It has to do with Karadzic and Krajisnik. You say on page 6, in the first paragraph: "My professional opinion is that Krajisnik and Karadzic used their positions for their personal benefit. They were involved in illegal financial transactions and money laundering. All the profits went to their overseas accounts. I remember the story that went around among the journalists. I mean that the Bosnian Minister Silajdzic met with Karadzic in a place between Pale and Sarajevo so that they would reach an agreement concerning the selling of certain parts of Bosnia. They decided that the Serbs should start shelling certain towns for about a million or a million and a half Deutschmark and that they should remain where they were." On the basis of what can you say an ugly thing like that in relation to Karadzic, that he was meeting with Silajdzic and that he was trying to sell parts of Bosnia for money? I mean, this is a very grave accusation. Is this what you really said? Do you have any grounds for this kind of assertion?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, that is what I said. Again, there is a mistake. It was not Karadzic, it was Krajisnik. Everything else that is contained in the statement is indeed what I said. And I got this knowledge from meetings with various people from the leadership of Republika Srpska and also having talked to some politicians from the area of the federation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That was rather more than your time as it is. Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zafirovic, I would like to ask you if you could just explain a few more things to the Judges. They have to do with your stay in Geneva. You speak about this in your statement, and it is on page 7 of the B/C/S version, and the English version is paragraph 6 on page 6. A few minutes ago during the cross-examination, you said that in Geneva there were three delegations. One was the Serb delegation. It was led by Karadzic; is that right? And the second one was the Muslim delegation. It was led by Karadzic -- by Izetbegovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And the third one was the Croat delegation that was led by Boban; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then the representatives of Serbia and Croatia were asked to mediate in these talks and to help as much as they could?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If you could explain now what you said a few minutes ago in response to the questions put to you by Prosecutor Groome you said that Slobodan Milosevic at the negotiations in Geneva was head of the delegation of the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, that was the impression that one invariably had when the accused was in Geneva. As I've already mentioned during my testimony, he had regular contact with the delegation of Republika Srpska in the periods when he was physically not present in Geneva. That was confirmed to me from several sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just tell me whether Slobodan Milosevic at that time could give any kind of orders to the representatives of the Serb side in those negotiations or whether he could have done anything against their will.

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is my deep conviction that at that time, the accused did have the possibility of affecting decisions of the leadership of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether he could decide anything on their behalf or give them orders.

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Formally, the decision had to be made by the leadership of Republika Srpska. Now, whether he could have ordered them to do so, that is something that I really did not know about. I did not attend their internal meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You say in your statement they called him in order to seek advice. Is that the right way of putting it?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: I stand by that, that there were regular communications between the accused and the delegation of Republika Srpska in Geneva.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, wasn't that the normal way to proceed? But here you say something that you did not say in your previous statement, that between them in communications when somebody addressed Slobodan Milosevic, they used the expression "Big Daddy" or "Boss."

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. These were informal talks between members of the delegations, their bodyguards, and lower-ranking officials who were in Geneva. When mentioning the accused, they used these words.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But you personally did not hear that?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: No, I did hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This is what --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Mr. May, just one. Perhaps it has to do with the translation. I don't think that Mr. Zafirovic means it that way. He said that that is how they addressed me. I assume that they did not address me directly. Nobody ever addressed me directly that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No one has said that. No one has said that it was directed to you personally. It was their own comments themselves informally. At least, that's what I understand. Yes, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't want to dwell on that much longer, but he said that everything he said here was what he knew about from his contacts with bodyguards, members of their security details, et cetera, but I don't want to go into all of that. In the next paragraph it says -- or, rather, you said here today that you saw when Mladic left the meeting at Milosevic's office.

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw General Mladic walking down the staircase in the building of the Presidency of Serbia, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And this is what you say in paragraph 7 on page 7: "Mladic came alone secretly to Belgrade to meet with Milosevic. He quietly entered the Serb Presidency building. There was no announcement, no press briefing, and no press notification of the visit." How do you explain that? Was this the way it was or was it the way that you had put it that way?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is exactly the way it was. This is how he entered the building. He quietly entered it, but then my previous reference was to the way he exited. I think I explained that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more thing. You said here today when -- that when you came to Bijeljina, you said that at the border, you saw 60 of Arkan's men, is that right, armed?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: I just have to correct this. It wasn't when I was coming to Bijeljina. It was two days prior to my arrival in Bijeljina, when I had set out for Bosnia-Herzegovina and when I did not reach Bijeljina. So the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: On the day when you arrived? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: On the day when I arrived. That was the 4th of April. On that day, at the border, I did not see members of the Serb Volunteer Guard; I saw them in Bijeljina itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more thing. You said a few minutes ago that the JNA had taken care of the refugees on that day. The refugees that were taken care of at the JNA barracks, were they both Muslims and Serbs?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: I do not have any precise information, but my answer could be yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more thing. In the streets on that day, were there any JNA soldiers at all?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: I've already answered that question, and the answer was no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have no re-examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Zafirovic, you remember that Arkan and Mr. Abdic at Bijeljina went to the Radio Bijeljina station and made a speech. Did you follow them there?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was there with the group of journalists that went towards Radio Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wonder whether you are in the position to confirm that Abdic's speech was broadcast at that time or not?

utterances.speaker: NENAD ZAFIROVIC
utterances.text: I can confirm that. To the best of my knowledge, this joint address of Fikret Abdic and Zeljko Raznjatovic Arkan was broadcast indeed, and it called for a calming down of the situation in town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Zafirovic, that concludes your evidence now. Thank you for coming here to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness, I think, is in closed session. Before we come to that might it be convenient to mention a few procedural matters and to do so swiftly by use of some speaking notes that I've had prepared that have the disadvantage of having the odd error in them but I think they're better than nothing. If they could be distributed and then I can be very brief and I hope we can accomplish the task of hearing both witnesses scheduled for this morning this morning. Because it is a somewhat imperfect document, I prefer not to file it but if it could be treated as strictly confidential by all parties I will avoid going into closed session, private -- or, rather, I'll avoid seeking to go into private session by not referring to names where they are dealt with in the document. And point number 1 is that the safe conduct request is now before you in a courtesy copy form. It's been filed. We ask if you're able to deal with it today it would be extremely helpful because until the documentation for safe conduct is in place, a seven-day period necessary to ensure the travel of the potential witness can't start to run. Paragraph 2. I've mentioned earlier that it may be the Chamber will think looking at the schedule of witnesses that certainty would be -- or near certainty would be helpful for us all, certainty as to which witnesses may be called, which may have to be dropped. And if the Chamber were to think it a good idea to give strict timetables in advance, I've set out under paragraph 2 for some witnesses, and I'll finish it I hope tomorrow, what we would say would be the maximum time that we would ask for for examination-in-chief. And incidentally, two-thirds of the way down the list two names read 3/4. That's three-quarters, it's not three or four hours. Paragraphs 3, 4, and 5 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before you get on to that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- Mr. Nice, I must say, speaking for myself, it's difficult to decide what may be important witnesses which you wish to call can necessarily be decided in a very generalised way without us really having any particular idea about this. I mean, I warn you of that. Of course we'll look at this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I can see that problem, of course. It's a question of balancing. The Chamber now sees the witnesses and the topics they cover on the schedule, and there may, in the Chamber's judgement, be an overall advantage in securing certainty that certain witnesses will be available, even if that means ensuring that the accused has his mind focused by limitations on cross-examination at an early stage. But I understand the point. Your Honour, witnesses -- points 3, 4, and 5 are outstanding rulings which would assist us, particularly 3, in relation to the Prijedor witnesses, and also 4. The Chamber will remember what I've said in the application which named that witness and why, in our respectful submission, his evidence should be before you but we simply don't have time to call him in full for he would be a very extensive witness if he was able to cover all matters on which we don't actually require him. Paragraph 6 relates to a particular form of intercept witness. We've already asked that if rejection is contemplated, we might be able to address you orally. Can I draw to your attention that the Prosecutor herself has been actively pursuing this matter? We haven't yet got a response, but the authorities have been subject to a quite direct request, and we'd ask for you to take that into account. Paragraph 7 relates to the camps project, and that application for documents to be exhibited without witness recall is one we'll be assisted by knowing the answer to. Paragraph 8, in light of the refusal of an 89(F) statement, understandably on the grounds of lateness of service, can we draw to your attention that this witness, due to testify on Friday, is only coming on Thursday so that there's no prospect of a signed statement in advance. Would a draft, on this occasion -- we know the views on drafts are somewhat -- they're not necessarily to favour them, but on this occasion might a draft assist, were the Chamber to notify of that by the end of today's hearings we could respond. Paragraph 10 deals with the intercept project. That's the Bosnian intercepts, and the Chamber will recall seeking a document that would identify in a sentence or so why a particular intercept should be admitted. I hope the schedule will be available tomorrow. His Honour Judge Kwon may like to know that the material we're working with is such that will enable us to sort it in various electronic ways, although it will be presented to the Chamber in one, or possibly two, hard copy formats. They substantially speak to themselves, although the schedule does rely to an extent on the expertise of a researcher, and so although a witness was refused, and where the four asterisks are the refusal by the Chamber was on grounds of relevance not being established. When the document is before you, as I hope it will be tomorrow or possibly Thursday, one issue will be whether the researcher should be available for cross-examination and if so, we would ask that that be limited in time for the accused to identify with particularity what interpretations he challenges. 11 is -- relates to the witness we've already spoken of in paragraph 1, and I remind the Chamber that this is a witness both who would be prefer to be called by the Chamber but whose interpretations may not coincide with those of the Prosecution, and we would invite the Chamber to allow him to deal with the very substantial quantity of documents that he can cover and which he will deal with briefly by perhaps scheduling entries that relate to common topics, and we would ask to be able to put in our interpretation, as we would have done in an opening statement had the documents been available then to get round the problem that I set out in paragraph 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's not clear to me. If you could explain to me what you mean by scheduling according to the Prosecution's interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, these particular documents -- and as we're in open session I'm going to speak somewhat obliquely -- cover topics that recur throughout the various different meetings that the documents cover. Now, it might be that the Prosecution would want to say, well, all these various passages relating to this particular topic show this objective on the part of the leadership, and so we would schedule them. We would say here's a topic. This topic is dealt with at this meeting, pages so-and-so, this meeting, pages so-and-so, this meeting, pages so-and-so, and the interpretation we would invite the Chamber to consider would be the following. The witness may offer evidence of a different kind. This is a witness not dissimilar from earlier witnesses we've called whose evidence will not necessarily be accepted by the Prosecution but who we are quite satisfied should be before you in general terms and because of his evidence overall. We have identified a constitutional expert. It's very remiss of me not to have got the name. I should inform the Chamber, and indeed the accused, he is a German academic. He's working in a Croatian institute, but he seems to us to be entirely suitable, and his report will be available but not, I think, with the margin of 30 days before the close of our case, and his name is not at present on the schedule of witnesses. 13 deals with a proof of death project in respect of Kosovo of which you may be unaware. It's been in preparation for a long time. It seeks to save labourious ploughing through the exhumation materials, and we'll provide by a spreadsheet identification of the way various deaths are dealt with. We're going to invite you to accept it without a witness being called. It will be with you soon. I hope by the end of next week. Paragraph 14. "Fill Box" documents and the chronology are going to continue to be provided. We will offer another one because I know that the amici in particular find it helpful. We will offer another version of all of those by the end of January, and we hope to have a final version for use in 98 bis arguments available almost immediately the Prosecution case closes. Our intention is to convert or to further convert these documents to the CaseMap format before the opening of the Defence case and thereafter to continue logging evidence in a way that will make a chronology and/or will make documents similar to Fill Box documents available periodically. And that brings me to paragraph 15, which is where we repeat the promise we've made earlier, namely that we will, before we engage in the process of conversion to CaseMap, set out our proposed list of topics by which material can be computer sorted to the parties and to the Chamber in case other views are thought to -- be or other views are advanced by which we can add to or change the topics by which we will make the material sortable. And then finally 16 and 17 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Pausing there. We are doing ours ourselves, but I wonder if you can produce a document which is called as dramatis personae which can be used as a starting point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We can do that, certainly, yes. And I think the proposal that we should offer in advance as criteria for CaseMap sorting, something we made right at the beginning, as soon as CaseMap became a possibility, I gather in other Chambers it's now become a requirement so we were not out of line with the practice in some Chambers, I think; it's agreed in advance what should be the criteria by which the material be sorted. But we'll certainly make dramatis personae as one of the -- or some of the dramatis personae. And then two points, 16 and 17. The Chamber will remember before we converted to the chart as the method of notifying witnesses, we had a three-part witness list which really set out our approach to witnesses and our intention in relation to witnesses for, I suppose, the last year or thereabouts, I'm not quite sure when it started. Part II of that list was witnesses who the Chamber would possibly or arguably like to hear from if time were not limited and it's always been our view that we should notify you of that sort of witness because otherwise, if the Chamber has any intention of exercising its powers to call witnesses on its own initiative, it wouldn't know who is available. I mention here one particular witness - I can name him: Mr. Arria. He's currently been removed from the schedule it not being clear whether there's time to call him or not. It seems to us that he's a witness who would be interesting to the Chamber. He's prepared a substantial history setting out the history and view of events of a leading member of the non-aligned group at the United Nations at the time. His report covers issues of foreseeability for Srebrenica and the massacre. It also covers embargoes and other Security Council resolutions and is extremely critical of the approach of the members of the Security Council and of the international community and it might be thought to provide insight otherwise not available. Now his report is quite extensive --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down a little.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. I apologise. The report is in final revision. At the moment, we simply can't be sure if there's time to call him, but we would suggest that it might be helpful for us to serve this report in the hope that it might be taken under 89(F) with limited cross-examination if time only allows for that. And then there's one other name which I won't read out, but his name can be seen on paragraph 17, and it seemed important to do two things about this person who has volunteered to give evidence. You will see his historical and present circumstances. And his material in written form, which we sought from him, has been made available to the accused and the amici. There's no prospect of our even considering calling him as a witness although we may see him in due course, but he's made it clear that his material, although confidential for the purposes of the Court, and you can see to what issues it generally goes, is available not only to the accused and the amici, on whom it's already been served, but to the Chamber should they want to see it now or at some later stage. And we're going to add his name to part B of the list because again, without our doing so, you simply wouldn't know that such a witness was available. That's all, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Does that conclude --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's all I want to draw to your attention and I'm simply trying to take as little time as possible to make sure that we make the best use of the remaining time in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You better tell us -- these elliptical matters are not always clear, and the number you were speaking to last.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Can we go into private session just for those purposes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The list of 20 witnesses that you have put forward in paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Are they already inside your schedule which has been served on us?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So they're included here. And how many new witnesses are there outside the number who are on the schedule?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's nothing outside the schedule. The two at the end of that list of 20, which says "If called - see below," Arria and Tromp, have -- Arria has been within the schedule at one stage and has been temporarily removed because it looks unlikely that we will be able to call him. Tromp is somebody you refused on the grounds that I already set out as relevance not established. That's the expert. But they're all on the schedule in the sense that they're either in the tabulated part of the schedule or in the footnotes at the bottom of witnesses to be added.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nice. Yes. I'm grateful to the Court, but -- yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, from what we have just heard and this list and the time available, it is quite obvious that Mr. Nice is abusing the fact that his time is running out in order to push in at great haste, topsy-turvy, as we would say, additional witnesses accompanied by an enormous amount of material while at the same time insisting on the maximum shortening of my cross-examination. This was also illustrated by the former example, and as far as I understand it, it will be repeated with the next witness. So I think it is absolutely unacceptable to limit so rigorously my time for cross-examination regardless of the witnesses in question if the side opposite feels that they should call them. And I think this is nothing more than abuse of the fact that they have no more time. And it is very hard to explain that since they have been presenting their half time for two years now, and they are now under pressure of time. I will not mention the name of Izetbegovic's associate that Mr. Nice mentioned at the end, because he says it is confidential. I haven't received any material regarding any statement by him, so could that be served on me, though it's probably of no importance, as many other things are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It will be a matter for the Trial Chamber to rule how long an accused is to have. It is open to the Prosecution to put forward, if they wish, a proposal as to how long they say, given the time which is available to them, how long the witness should have in a particular case. But at the same time, it's the responsibility, of course, of the Prosecution, the Prosecution to make one point, but also, of course, for the Trial Chamber, which ultimately have to determine, and that's why the Prosecution will make its submission but it's the Trial Chamber which make a decision which ensure that there is a reasonable time. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I shall be very brief in view of time constraints. It is very hard at this point in time to express an opinion regarding everything that Mr. Nice has covered. Of course on behalf of the amici, I can say that we stand by our principled positions that we have advocated so far. I would just appeal to you for one thing. As Mr. Kay is not present today, he will be here on Thursday, it seems to me that perhaps after consultations with him we might have certain observations to make regarding point 12, because here it is stated that a German academic is being called as an expert witness for constitutional matters, but it is stated that he's working in a Croatian institute. I don't know whether we will object along those lines, but I would like to reserve our position on that until Thursday. What I am concerned by as an amicus, you have already ruled on it so I won't go into it, but the witness referred to under paragraph 1 will be examined pursuant to your decision, but I think that everything connected to this witness will require more time than is available, but we will do our best to cross-examine that witness as best we can in the time available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We will consider about this in due course. We're not going to make a ruling about that at the moment. Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Only to say, Your Honour, that the accused has had notice of all these witnesses in advance, save the one covered in paragraph 1 who was notified as soon as he was available. And he may be working under a misunderstanding because he sometimes doesn't focus on procedural matters. In paragraph 2 we are setting out maximum examination-in-chief times we would seek were the Chamber to decide to make strict timetable rulings, that's all. The next witness is subject to protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In fact, we're not going to reach him before the adjournment. There are two matters I want to deal with. If the officers for the Tribunal would come up, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: As far as the next witness is concerned, these are not matters in open court. Anything you want to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, but I remember that in respect of Mr. Tapuskovic's observation about the proposed expert, the Chamber will remember that it is the expert we've been able to identify after having very considerable difficulties, and the proposed response, which is the sort of thing that I'm afraid I've rather anticipated is inappropriate. I drew it to everybody's attention because I feared that sort of response might be forthcoming, but this is an expert of international reputability, and it would be quite wrong to suggest that he could be excluded on grounds basically of prejudice. So I'm disturbed and saddened to hear that preliminary indication by the amici. Nothing else, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It will be a matter for the Trial Chamber to determine, which we'll do. No. We've finished now. We're going to adjourn for a quarter of an hour -- 20 minutes, rather, and then we'll continue in the usual rules. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: be reconvened on Thursday, the 15th day of January, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.
